Theme

how old are you? phrase

also how old

classical

Quot annōrum es?

question: the genitive of quality, “of how many years are you?”

Other words

  • Quot annōs nātus (nāta) es? — how old are you?

    also used · classical

    Answered in the same form: Trēs annōs nātus sum, I’m three. The ordinal with agō counts the year one is in, which is one more: the same child quārtum annum agit, is in his fourth year, since the first year runs from birth to the first birthday (see age).

Examples

  • Baba ferē nōnāgintā annōs nāta est, lenta quidem, sed suīs pedibus ambulat.

    Baba is nearly ninety, slow indeed, but she walks on her own feet.Libellus VII, Diēs ūnus Osoitsae

  • quattuor et vīgintī fermē annōs nātus

    about twenty-four years oldLiv. 26.18.7

  • Decem annōs est nātus. Ūndecimum agit (aetātis annum).

    He’s ten: he is in his eleventh year.Fōrm. VI 19

See also two years old, three years old, age, a man of.

SourcesThe phrase is composed; the grouped card gave no source.

Theodōrus et pater · Ad Larem avītum, Libellī I–VII, as they stood on 7 November 2026, with their glosses. Examples marked “Libellus” quote those texts word for word; classical passages are cited by author.

Fōrm. VI 19 is from the Latīnitās loci collection of Franmōrārius, Dē variīs Latīnīs Graecīsque colloquendī fōrmulīs, a modern book; the classical instances are cited beside it.
